selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on whether representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matter, and no reference level of performance. 2) This run sets a simple, interpretable baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a standard PCA (2000) representation and no aggregation or fusion. Later runs can each change one factor against it, such as the RNA encoder (config_001 scVI, config_048 scGPT), the modality (image-only), the profile setting (config_030 multiprofile avgpool) or adding images (config_038/config_005). 3) Starting with a complex multimodal, multiprofile model would mix many design choices in one result and would not show whether the added complexity helps. A cheap, low-variance anchor makes every later comparison easier to interpret, which is the most informative use of the first experiment under a limited budget.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one result exists. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n2000) baseline reached about 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. So we know nothing yet about how profile setting, encoder, aggregation, modality or fusion affect performance. 2. What this tests: config_030 keeps the model setting (RNA-only) and encoder (PCA n2000) the same and changes only the profile setting from single to multi. It uses the simplest aggregation, avgpool. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, without adding transformer or fusion complexity. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: profile setting is a structural choice that affects most of the remaining configurations. A clean one-factor comparison against the existing baseline will show whether the multiprofile part of the space is worth exploring. Encoder, modality and fusion comparisons can follow.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool improved the RNA-only PCA model substantially (0.536 to 0.688 accuracy, 0.516 to 0.659 F1). This suggests profile setting matters a lot. Whether adding the image modality helps is the largest untested design question, since no image-containing model has been run. 2. What this tests: config_019 keeps the best-known setup fixed (PCA RNA encoder, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only a ResNet50 image encoder with the simplest fusion, concat. Comparing it directly to config_030 isolates the effect of multimodality. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: About half the search space is multimodal, so the result has high value for deciding where to search. If images help, later runs can refine the image encoder (ViT-L) and fusion (weighted). If they do not, the budget can shift to RNA encoder and aggregation choices (e.g., config_010, config_003, config_045).

1. Evidence: Multiprofile RNA-only with PCA and avgpool (config_030) is clearly the best so far, at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Its single-profile counterpart (config_020) reached only 0.536, which is strong evidence that profile setting matters. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_019) dropped performance to 0.532. That suggests the image branch or the fusion method hurts under the current setup, but one run cannot say which. 2. Test: config_010 keeps the best configuration fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, PCA) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention over profiles adds value beyond mean pooling. 3. Why now: with a limited budget, this extends the one strongly supported direction while still answering a clean design question. Aggregation applies to every multiprofile model, including the multimodal ones, so the result shapes many later choices. The other candidates, such as weighted fusion (config_015) or swapping the RNA encoder, are better run once the strongest RNA-only baseline and its aggregation are established.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile with PCA and avgpool (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1). Moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool helped clearly. Transformer aggregation (0.512) and adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion (0.532) both hurt. The RNA encoder is the main design axis not yet tested, since every run so far used pca_n2000. 2. Test: Swapping only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 in the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) isolates the effect of the RNA representation. It shows whether the strong result depends on PCA or holds for a learned latent representation. 3. Why now: This builds on the strongest direction found so far and resolves a major untested choice with a one-variable change. The result will also tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later fusion experiments (for example, weighted fusion). That makes it a better use of the limited budget than further multimodal runs, which so far have shown no benefit.

1. Evidence: The strongest setup so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, with avgpool aggregation. PCA in this setup reached 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659), and scVI reached 0.635 (F1 0.618). Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile (PCA singleprofile: 0.536), and transformer aggregation did worse than avgpool (0.512). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion also performed poorly (0.532). The RNA encoder comparison is still incomplete because scGPT has not been tested in this pipeline. 2. Test: config_003 changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT and keeps the best profile setting and aggregation. This finishes the encoder comparison and shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation can beat PCA. 3. Why now: Unresolved multimodal questions, such as weighted fusion or image-only baselines, matter less than confirming the best RNA backbone. It is a clean one-variable comparison with a real chance of a new best result, and it fixes the RNA encoder that later fusion experiments should build on.

Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_019) dropped accuracy to 0.532. That drop is unexplained. The image features may be uninformative, or concat fusion may be letting noisy image features swamp the strong RNA signal. This experiment keeps everything from config_019 the same and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only result, the earlier drop was mainly a fusion problem and multimodal models are worth pursuing. If accuracy stays near 0.53, the image features or the image encoder are the likely cause. Fusion choice applies to every multimodal configuration left in the pool, so this single-variable comparison is the cheapest way to decide whether that large part of the search space deserves more budget.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (0.688 acc). Multiprofile with avgpool clearly beats singleprofile and transformer aggregation. Among RNA encoders, PCA leads scVI, which leads scGPT. In the multimodal runs, weighted fusion (0.650) is far better than concat (0.532), but it still trails RNA-only. Every image experiment so far has used resnet50, so the image encoder is the main untested design choice. 2) Test: config_018 matches the best multimodal run (config_015: PCA, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) except that it swaps resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. This isolates the image encoder effect. It will show whether a stronger image representation lets fusion add information beyond RNA, or whether the image modality contributes little regardless of encoder. 3) Why now: it is a single-variable change on the most promising multimodal setup. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 images to that same RNA setup lowered accuracy, to 0.650 with weighted fusion and 0.532 with concat. ViT-L images did worse still, at 0.520. No image-only model has been run, so we cannot tell whether images carry little signal or whether the fusion step is the problem. 2) Test: config_043 is the image-only counterpart of the best multimodal run (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool), so it isolates how much predictive signal the image modality has on its own. 3) Why now: This baseline determines whether further multimodal and fusion experiments are worth the budget. If image-only is weak, we can focus on RNA-side choices such as the encoder and aggregation. 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile PCA with avgpool (0.688). Within multimodal models, fusion matters a lot: with PCA, ResNet50 and avgpool, weighted fusion (config_015) reached 0.650, while concat (config_019) reached only 0.532. scVI also performed reasonably in the RNA-only avgpool setting (0.635). It is still unclear whether adding images ever beats RNA alone, or whether this depends on the RNA encoder. 2) This experiment keeps the best multimodal recipe (multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI. That gives two clean single-variable comparisons. Against config_015, it isolates the effect of the RNA encoder under weighted fusion. Against config_045, it isolates the effect of adding image features through weighted fusion to scVI-based RNA. 3) It exploits the most promising multimodal direction while answering whether the weighted-fusion gain generalizes beyond PCA. This is more informative than options that repeat transformer aggregation, which has hurt so far, or concat fusion, which has underperformed.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment has been run. config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + ImageNet ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1. With no baseline, we cannot tell whether the image branch adds anything, which is the most basic design question. 2) What this tests: config_006 is the RNA-only counterpart of config_038. 1. Evidence: The multimodal scGPT + ViT-L model (avgpool, concat, multiprofile) reached 0.530 accuracy and 0.515 F1. The matching RNA-only scGPT model reached only 0.227 accuracy and 0.191 F1. This suggests the image modality may carry most of the signal, but we cannot tell whether RNA adds anything beyond images. 2. Test: config_026 is the image-only ViT-L model with the same profile setting (multiprofile) and aggregation (avgpool) as config_038. It completes the modality ablation. If it scores close to 0.53, fusion adds little and further search should focus on image encoders and aggregation. If it scores clearly lower, RNA is complementary and exploring fusion and RNA encoders is worthwhile. 3. Why now: Only one factor changes relative to existing runs, so the comparison is clean. It answers the most important open question, which modalities matter, and that answer shapes how the remaining budget should be spent.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal scGPT + ViT-L with avgpool and concat (0.530 accuracy, 0.515 F1). It only modestly beats image-only ViT-L (0.512 / 0.477). RNA-only scGPT is weak (0.227). So the image branch does most of the work, and RNA representation is the biggest open question: scGPT may simply be a poor RNA encoder for this task. 2. Test: config_042 keeps everything from the best run (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder from scGPT to PCA (n=2000). This isolates the effect of RNA representation on fused performance. If accuracy and F1 rise, the RNA encoder is the bottleneck and worth exploring further, including scVI. If they do not, RNA likely adds little regardless of encoder, and later experiments should focus on aggregation, fusion, or image encoder. 3. Why now: it is a one-variable change from the current best, so it serves two purposes. It tests a design choice with high uncertainty and potentially large impact, and it has a realistic chance of improving the best score. That makes it more informative than adjusting aggregation or fusion first, when the RNA branch may be what is holding the model back.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image features carry most of the signal. Image-only ViT-L reached 0.512 accuracy, while RNA-only scGPT reached only 0.227. Adding RNA gives a small gain (about 0.53). Swapping scGPT for PCA2000 in the multimodal model changed almost nothing (0.530 vs 0.532), so the RNA encoder looks minor here. Aggregation, fusion and profile setting are all untested, and every run so far used avgpool with concat. 2. What this tests: config_040 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, relative to the current best (config_042: multiprofile, PCA2000, ViT-L, concat). This isolates whether learned attention over the multiple profiles improves on simple mean pooling. 3. Why it is the best next run: aggregation is a central design choice for the multiprofile setting. A single-variable change from the best configuration is both informative and a reasonable bet for higher performance. Testing fusion or the image encoder next would then build on whichever aggregation wins.

1. Evidence: All five experiments so far used the multiprofile setting. Image features carry most of the signal: image-only scored 0.512 versus 0.227 for RNA-only. Multimodal concat adds only a little, reaching about 0.53. RNA encoder (scGPT vs PCA) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) changed accuracy by less than 0.01. So these choices look minor. Profile setting is still completely untested and is a major open design question. 2. Test: config_025 matches the current best, config_042 (PCA-2000, ViT-L, concat), except it uses a single profile. Aggregation is necessarily None in that setting. This isolates whether multiprofile input actually helps, or whether a simpler single-profile model performs as well. 3. Why now: Further tweaks to RNA encoder or aggregation are unlikely to be informative given the small differences seen so far. Resolving profile setting, an axis with no data yet, removes more uncertainty and tells us which part of the search space to exploit with the remaining budget.

1) Evidence: single-profile multimodal (config_025: pca_n2000 + ViT-L, concat) reached 0.713 accuracy. Every multiprofile variant sat at about 0.51–0.53, so the profile setting looks like the dominant factor. In the multiprofile setting, adding RNA to ViT-L image features helped only slightly (0.512 image-only vs about 0.53 multimodal), and scGPT RNA-only was weak (0.227). 2) Test: config_048 is the single-profile, image-only ViT-L counterpart of config_025. It tells us whether RNA fusion adds real value in the best-performing regime or whether most of the gain comes from the single-profile image representation. 3) Why now: it changes only one factor (dropping RNA) from the current best configuration. The answer determines whether the remaining budget should go to tuning the RNA encoder and fusion method in single-profile multimodal models, or to image-encoder choices.

1. Evidence: the single-profile multimodal model (config_025, PCA-2000 RNA + ViT-L, concat) is by far the best at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. The single-profile image-only model (config_048) reached only 0.523, so most of the gain appears to come from adding RNA in the single-profile setting. In the multiprofile setting, RNA added almost nothing over image alone, and scGPT RNA alone was weak (0.227). The uncertainty is whether the 0.713 comes from true multimodal fusion or mostly from single-profile PCA RNA features on their own. 2. Test: config_031 is PCA-2000 RNA-only in the single-profile setting. It differs from config_025 only by removing the image branch, which completes the RNA-only / image-only / multimodal comparison for that setting. This isolates the contribution of each modality and of fusion. 3. Why now: the result will guide the rest of the budget. If RNA-only comes close to 0.71, later experiments should focus on RNA encoders such as scVI and scGPT. If it falls well short, fusion matters, and later experiments should refine the fusion method and image encoder around config_025.

1. Evidence: The singleprofile multimodal model (config_025: pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, concat) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. That is far above every multiprofile run (about 0.53) and above either single-modality singleprofile baseline (image 0.523, RNA 0.494). So singleprofile multimodal is the clear lead direction. Within multiprofile, the RNA encoder (scgpt vs pca) and aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) made little difference. Fusion has never been varied, because every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. Test: config_008 keeps config_025 identical and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. It directly isolates the effect of fusion in the best-performing setting. 3. Why now: fusion is the one design dimension with no evidence at all, and the clean single-variable comparison is anchored to the strongest result. It may also improve on the current best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. RNA encoder swaps in singleprofile (scvi or scgpt) are the logical next step after this.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_025 (singleprofile, pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, concat fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. That is far above every other run, which all fall around 0.49–0.53. Its weighted-fusion counterpart scored only 0.525, so concat fusion in the singleprofile setting looks central to the gain. However, every run with images so far has used imagenet_vit_l. Whether the image representation matters, and whether the 0.713 result holds up beyond one encoder, is still unknown. 2. Test: config_013 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50. This isolates the effect of image representation in the most promising region of the search space. 3. Why now: It builds on the strongest result while reducing a large, entirely unexplored uncertainty, since resnet50 has never been evaluated. It also checks whether the singleprofile + concat advantage is robust rather than a one-off. Testing alternative RNA encoders (scvi_n200, scgpt) in this setting are logical follow-ups.

1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we have no information about how modality, RNA representation, profile setting, aggregation or fusion affect performance. 2. What it tests: The simplest configuration (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000, no aggregation or fusion) sets a baseline for validation accuracy and F1. Its single-factor neighbors let us isolate each design choice later: config_013 for multiprofile vs. single-profile, config_036 and config_011 for scVI and scGPT vs. PCA, and config_035 and config_028 for adding images. 3. Why now: Starting with the simplest model avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile setups help. It anchors the search in a way that makes later controlled comparisons interpretable, which is the best use of the first experiment on a limited budget.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_031) at about 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Profile setting, aggregation, fusion, and the other encoders are all untested. 2) This experiment keeps the RNA encoder fixed at pca_n2000 and switches to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. Because only one factor changes, it cleanly measures whether multiprofile inputs help, which is a central design choice in this search. 3) The single-profile versus multiprofile question applies to every modality and model setting, so answering it first has the most downstream value. Testing it with the simplest aggregation and a known encoder avoids mixing several effects together, and the result will guide whether later experiments should invest in multiprofile and multimodal variants.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested so far. Single-profile (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1) slightly beat multiprofile with avgpool (0.639 acc, 0.620 F1). That gap is small and comes from one comparison, so the profile question is not settled. The larger open question is whether adding image data helps at all. 2. What this tests: config_028 keeps the best known setting fixed (single-profile, PCA n2000 RNA encoder) and adds one change, an imagenet_vit_l image encoder joined to the RNA features by simple concat fusion. Comparing it directly with config_031 shows the value of adding the image modality, without changes to aggregation or profile setting muddying the result. 3. Why this is the best use of budget: Whether to use the image modality decides which half of the remaining configurations is worth pursuing. Answering it now, with a clean single-variable comparison, avoids spending budget on multimodal or image-only variants if images do not help, and justifies exploring them if they do. Encoder and aggregation refinements can follow once this is known.

1. Evidence: The two RNA-only PCA runs are close (single-profile 0.650, multiprofile avgpool 0.639), so profile setting has only a small effect so far. Adding ImageNet ViT-L image features with concat fusion dropped accuracy to 0.520, with F1 falling by a similar amount. That is the largest effect observed. It is unclear whether the drop comes from the fusion method, with concat possibly letting noisy image features swamp the RNA signal, or from multimodal integration itself. 2. Test: config_016 keeps everything from config_028 the same (single-profile, PCA, ViT-L) and only switches concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers to RNA-only levels or above, multimodal models are still worth pursuing with weighted fusion. If it stays low, image features likely hurt here and the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. 3. Why now: it is a one-variable comparison on the biggest unexplained effect, and its answer decides whether a large share of the remaining multimodal configurations is worth the budget.

1. Evidence: Weighted fusion clearly beat concat with the same singleprofile PCA + ViT-L backbone (0.678 vs 0.520 accuracy, with F1 agreeing). That makes config_016 the current best and suggests fusion choice matters a lot. Profile setting is less clear. For RNA-only, multiprofile avgpool was only slightly worse than singleprofile (0.639 vs 0.650), which is too small a gap to treat as conclusive, and it may not carry over to multimodal models. 2. Test: config_026 keeps the best setup (PCA, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This shows whether multiprofile helps or hurts once weighted fusion is in place. 3. Why now: It is a minimal, controlled extension of the best configuration, so it has a reasonable chance of improving accuracy. It also answers a central design question (single vs multiprofile in multimodal models) that will guide many of the remaining untested configurations.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal PCA + ViT-L with weighted fusion (config_016, acc 0.678, F1 0.646). Multiprofile with avgpool has hurt in both settings tested. The drop is small for RNA-only (0.650 to 0.639) but large for multimodal weighted fusion (0.678 to 0.535). We do not yet know whether multiprofile itself is unhelpful or whether avgpool is the problem, since mean pooling may wash out profile-specific signal. 2. What this tests: config_049 changes only the aggregation (avgpool to transformer) relative to config_026, keeping PCA, ViT-L, weighted fusion and multiprofile fixed. If accuracy recovers toward or above 0.678, aggregation is the bottleneck and learned multiprofile aggregation is worth pursuing. If it stays near 0.535, that is strong evidence that single-profile is preferable here. Either way, a large branch of the search space can be pruned. 3. Why now: The profile and aggregation question governs most of the remaining configurations, so resolving it is worth more than a small encoder swap around the current best. Encoder swaps can follow once we know which profile setting to focus on.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.715, F1 0.687). Its avgpool counterpart, config_026, scored much lower (0.535). For RNA-only models, multiprofile with avgpool (0.639) slightly underperformed singleprofile (0.650). So avgpool looks harmful and transformer aggregation looks helpful, but transformer aggregation has only been tested together with image features and weighted fusion. We cannot yet tell whether the gain comes from the aggregation method or from how it interacts with multimodal fusion.
2. What this tests: config_033 is the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA model with transformer aggregation. It differs from config_013 only in aggregation (avgpool vs transformer), which isolates the aggregation effect. It also serves as a unimodal baseline under the best aggregation, showing how much of config_049's 0.715 is due to adding image features.
3. Why it is the best use of the next experiment: Aggregation is the design choice with the largest observed effect, and the multiprofile-vs-singleprofile question depends on it. The fusion question already has clearer evidence: weighted fusion beat concat by a wide margin in the singleprofile comparison. This single-variable experiment therefore resolves a major uncertainty before spending budget on encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ResNet50) around the current best.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), with 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Transformer aggregation behaved very differently by modality. It collapsed for RNA-only (config_033, 0.26) but was best for multimodal. Weighted fusion also clearly beat concat in the single-profile setting (0.678 vs 0.520). However, no image-only model has been tested, so we cannot tell whether the multiprofile transformer gain comes from the image features or from real RNA+image complementarity. 2. What this tests: config_048 is the image-only version of config_049 (same multiprofile setting, ViT-L encoder and transformer aggregation, RNA removed). It is a single-factor ablation that directly measures how much the RNA branch adds to the current best model. It also shows whether transformer aggregation works well specifically for image profiles. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The result guides the next steps either way. If image-only is close to 0.715, later budget should go to image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders. If it falls well short, fusion is shown to matter, and swapping RNA encoders in the best configuration (e.g., config_050 with scvi_n200) becomes the clear next move. Testing an RNA encoder first would build on a component whose contribution has not yet been established.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.715, F1 0.687). Weighted fusion has clearly beaten concat in the matched single-profile comparison (0.678 vs 0.520). Every experiment so far has used pca_n2000 for RNA, so the RNA encoder is completely unexplored. RNA appears to be the stronger modality (RNA-only 0.65 vs image-only 0.51), so the RNA representation is likely an important choice. Test: config_050 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 to scvi_n200) and keeps the best configuration otherwise fixed. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation in the most promising setting. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while closing a major gap in knowledge with a single-variable comparison. Either outcome tells us whether further gains should come from the RNA representation or from other factors, such as the image encoder.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion; acc 0.715, F1 0.687). Single-variable comparisons already favor PCA over scVI (0.537), weighted over concat fusion (0.678 vs 0.520 in singleprofile), and transformer over avgpool aggregation (0.715 vs 0.535). The image encoder has never been varied: every image-based run used ViT-L, and ResNet50 is completely untested. 2) Test: This run swaps ViT-L for ResNet50 and keeps everything else in the best configuration fixed. That isolates the effect of the image representation, which is the largest remaining unknown. 3) Value: It exploits the strongest setup while resolving an unexplored design axis. If ResNet50 matches or beats ViT-L, it opens a new branch to search. If it underperforms, it confirms that ViT-L should be the image encoder for the remaining budget. Either result is informative, which makes this more useful than retesting fusion or aggregation, where some evidence already exists.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence on which design choices (modality, profile setting, RNA or image encoder, aggregation, fusion) matter. 2) config_013 (multimodal, single profile, scVI RNA encoder, ViT-L image encoder, concat fusion) is a central anchor. 1. Evidence: Only one run exists. The single-profile multimodal model (scVI-200 RNA + ImageNet ViT-L, concat fusion) reached 0.514 accuracy and 0.498 F1. That gives one reference point but says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_050 keeps the same encoders and concat fusion and switches only to the multiprofile setting. Multiprofile requires an aggregation method, so it uses avgpool, the simplest one. This isolates the effect of profile setting, likely one of the largest structural choices in the space, without adding transformer aggregation or a different fusion method. 3. Why now: The result decides whether the large multiprofile part of the search space deserves more of the budget. If it clearly helps, later runs can compare transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and encoder swaps against this baseline. If it does not help, the search can focus on single-profile models and unimodal ablations such as config_010 and config_002.

1. Evidence: Only two experiments exist, and they differ in a single factor (profile setting). Both use scVI_n200 with ImageNet ViT-L and concat fusion. Moving from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.514 to 0.725 and F1 from 0.498 to 0.685. This is strong early evidence that multiprofile modeling matters. However, it is still uncertain whether a more expressive aggregator would capture more of that benefit, since avgpool is the simplest option. 2. Test: config_005 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, while keeping config_050's encoders, fusion and profile setting. This isolates the effect of the aggregation method within the most promising direction found so far. 3. Why now: Aggregation only applies in the multiprofile setting, which showed the largest effect, so resolving it next is a natural exploit-and-learn step. Whichever aggregator wins becomes a better base for later single-factor ablations of fusion, encoders and modality. Those ablations then avoid tuning several choices on top of a possibly suboptimal pooling choice.

1. Evidence: All three runs used scVI + ViT-L with concat fusion.
